summary: For ages 9–11: an ocean ecosystem is an interconnected system where living parts (producers, consumers, decomposers) and non-living factors (temperature, salinity, light, currents) interact, so a change to one part ripples through the whole. The core learning move is perturbation: change ONE factor and trace the multi-step, sometimes indirect consequences. Activities build from naming living/non-living parts (Tier A), to linking a non-living factor to the living community (Tier B), to tracing a cascade through several steps (Tier C). A manipulable ecosystem model is the centrepiece, supported by a labelled systems diagram, targeted checks, and what-if dialogue.
misconceptions: Thinking an ecosystem is just the animals/plants (biotic) and forgetting the non-living factors that shape it.
Believing effects are local and direct — not anticipating indirect, multi-step, or distant ripples.
Confusing a food web (energy among organisms) with an ecosystem (organisms + physical environment as one system).
Ignoring decomposers/recycling, treating the system as a one-way flow rather than a cycle.
Assuming ecosystems are static/balanced forever rather than dynamic systems that respond to change.

activities.title: Run the kelp forest: perturb one factor, trace the ripple
steps: Explore a kelp-forest model with adjustable factors for water temperature, light, salinity and current, and a community of producers (phytoplankton, the plant-like plankton, and kelp), consumers (zooplankton, urchins, fish, sea otters) and decomposers.
Change ONE factor only — e.g. nudge the water warmer — and watch over time how the community responds step by step.
Before each change, predict out loud which living thing will be hit first and what will follow two or three steps along the chain.

After watching, trace the actual chain in order (for example: warmer water → plankton thin out → the plankton-feeders that ate them dwindle → their predators go hungry → decomposer workload shifts) and compare it with your prediction. Treat this as one plausible outcome, not the only one.
Run several different perturbations (e.g. cloudier water so less light gets through) and note any effect that surprised you or reached a creature you would not have connected to that factor.
State in your own words why touching just one non-living factor moved the whole web.
activities.insight: An ocean ecosystem is living AND non-living parts locked together; changing one factor cascades through multiple steps, and effects can be indirect and surprising rather than staying contained to one species.

activities.title: Map the system: living and non-living parts linked
steps: Study a labelled ecosystem web showing producers, consumers, decomposers and the non-living factors (temperature, salinity, light, currents).
Select a non-living factor (e.g. temperature or light) and identify which organisms it affects and how.
Sketch or describe at least one first-order effect: 'if this rose, then ...'.
Add the decomposers and show how they return matter to the system, making it a cycle rather than a one-way chain.
activities.insight: An ecosystem's parts — living and non-living — are connected into a structure, and non-living factors are members of the system, not just a backdrop.

activities.title: Check your understanding: parts, definitions and cascades
steps: Sort items into living and non-living parts of the ecosystem.
Name the key non-living factors that affect ocean life: temperature, salinity, light, currents.
Distinguish a food web (energy among organisms) from an ecosystem (organisms plus their physical environment as one system).
Given a scenario — e.g. the water warms a few degrees for a whole season — trace the multi-step ripple and explain whether the effect stays contained.
activities.insight: Confirms the learner can name the system's parts, tell a food web from an ecosystem, and follow a change through several steps rather than only naming isolated parts.

activities.title: What-if with a marine ecologist: predict the chain
steps: Respond to a marine ecologist (real or role-played) posing 'what happens if the water warms?' or 'what if less light gets through?'
Predict the chain of consequences aloud, step by step, before any answer is revealed.

Answer probing follow-ups: name one living thing hit first, then follow the chain to something two steps away; identify which non-living parts could change the animals; judge whether a small change could tip the whole system into something different.
activities.insight: Articulating a cascade in conversation surfaces whether the learner can follow a connected chain or only name isolated parts.

checkQuestion: In a kelp-forest ecosystem the water warms up by a few degrees for a whole season. A child says 'the only thing that changes is the animals that don't like warm water — everything else stays the same'. Do you think a change to just the temperature would stay contained like that? Talk me through what happens, and why.
checkAnswer: No — an ecosystem is a system where living things and non-living factors (temperature, salinity, light, currents) all interact, so a change in one factor ripples through the whole thing. Warmer water can weaken the kelp (a producer), or make plankton bloom or crash; that changes food for the animals that eat them, which changes their predators, and it can also change which species can survive there at all. Because the parts are connected, a change to one non-living factor cascades — it doesn't stay contained to a single species.
